To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the volume of tweets from users and MPs is a good indicator of their voting intention, 2) the volume of user tweets is a good indicator for the popularity of the key issues, 3) the sentiment of user tweets is not a reliable indicator of their voting intentions and 4) the sentiment of the tweets is not a good indicator for popularity of key issues.
• The sentiment analysis of the tweets from the UK MPs is not a good proxy for their voting intentions.
the sentiment analysis of UK MP tweets towards political parties is accurate, but not sufficiently accurate for predicting voting intention.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new forms of automated opinion polling using Twitter.
the development of new techniques for the automated analysis of political tweets, and the evaluation of their accuracy and utility for passive opinion polling.
the automated analysis of Twitter data in order to understand how people use Twitter for discussing politics, to identify key topics, to detect sentiment and to infer voting intentions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of Twitter as a source for opinion polling is feasible, but not yet accurate enough to be used in place of traditional polling techniques.

Twitter provides a useful resource for the automated monitoring of the political discourse and sentiment on the UK political scene, and that it is a useful tool for the automatic identification of key issues and the general sentiment towards the parties.
the results are promising but not conclusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to automatically detect key political issues and infer voting intentions with an accuracy that is comparable to traditional opinion polls.

the volume and sentiment analysis of the tweets from the MPs is a useful tool for monitoring their political activities, but that the tweets of the general public do not provide a good proxy for the voting intention of the UK public.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to automatically monitor and detect key political issues and infer voting intentions from Twitter data.
Twitter can provide a useful proxy for traditional opinion polls and can be used to automatically identify the main political issues discussed on Twitter and the sentiment of users towards them.
Twitter provides a useful resource for ‘passive’ polling of public opinion and that automated methods can provide useful results, although they need to be used with care.
